items.title: Beings' Lifespans Are Not Fixed Like the World's

items.zh: 若有情數，時無決定。所以者何？由彼造作種種業故，或過一劫，或復減少乃至一歲。
items.en: As for the lifespans of beings, however, their duration is not fixed. Why is this? Because beings create karma of many different kinds, a lifespan may exceed a full eon, or may be reduced to as little as a single year.

items.title: Three Calamities That Destroy the World

items.zh: 又彼壞劫。由三種災。一者、火災，能壞世間，從無間獄乃至梵世。二者、水災，能壞一切，乃至第二靜慮。三者、風災，能壞一切、乃至第三靜慮。第四靜慮無災能壞。由彼諸天身與宮殿俱生俱沒故，更無能壞因緣法故。復有三災之頂。謂第二靜慮、第三靜慮、第四靜慮。
items.en: Further, that eon of destruction comes about through three kinds of calamity. The first is fire, which destroys the world from the hell of uninterrupted suffering up to the Brahmā heavens. The second is water, which destroys everything up to the second dhyāna heaven. The third is wind, which destroys everything up to the third dhyāna heaven. The fourth dhyāna heaven is destroyed by no calamity at all, because the bodies of its gods arise and cease together with their own palaces, and there is simply no cause capable of destroying it. There are, moreover, three peaks of calamity: the second dhyāna, the third dhyāna, and the fourth dhyāna.

items.title: How Long a Great Eon Lasts

items.zh: 又此世間二十中劫壞，二十中劫壞已空，二十中劫成，二十中劫成已住；如是八十中劫，假立為一大劫數。
items.en: Further, in this world, twenty intermediate eons make up the eon of destruction; twenty more, once destroyed, make up the eon of emptiness; twenty more make up the eon of formation; and twenty more, once formed, make up the eon of abiding. These eighty intermediate eons together are provisionally called one great eon.

items.zh: 又梵世間壽量一劫，此最後壞，亦最初成。當知此劫異相建立。謂梵眾天，二十中劫合為一劫，即依此劫施設壽量。梵前益天，四十中劫合為一劫，即依此劫施設壽量。
items.en: Further, the lifespan in the Brahmā heavens is a full eon — this realm is the last to be destroyed, and the first to be formed. It should be understood that this "eon" is established differently at each level. For the multitude of Brahmā, twenty intermediate eons together make one eon, and their lifespan is reckoned by this eon. For the ministers of Brahmā, forty intermediate eons together make one eon, and their lifespan is reckoned by this eon.

items.title: One Intermediate Eon: A Rise and Fall Driven by Conduct

items.zh: 若大梵天，六十中劫合為一劫，即依此劫施設壽量。云何火災能壞世間？謂有如是時，世間有情壽量無限。從此漸減，乃至壽量經八萬歲。彼復受行不善法故，壽量轉減，乃至十歲。彼復獲得厭離之心，受行善法，由此因緣，壽量漸增，乃至八萬。如是壽量一減一增，合成一中劫。
items.en: As for Great Brahmā, sixty intermediate eons together make one eon, and his lifespan is reckoned by this eon. How does fire come to destroy the world? There is a time when the lifespan of beings in the world is unlimited. From this it gradually decreases, down to a lifespan of eighty thousand years. Then, because beings take up unwholesome practices, their lifespan decreases further, down to ten years. Then, having gained a mind of renunciation, they take up wholesome practices, and through this their lifespan gradually increases again, up to eighty thousand years. Such a single decrease and increase together make up one intermediate eon.

items.title: Two of the Three Minor Calamities: Famine and Disease

items.zh: 又此中劫，復有三種小災出現。謂儉、病、刀。儉災者，所謂人壽三十歲時，方始建立。當爾之時，精妙飲食不可復得，唯煎煮朽骨共為讌會。若遇得一粒稻、麥、粟、稗等子，重若末尼，藏置箱篋而守護之。
items.en: Further, within this intermediate eon, three minor calamities occur: famine, disease, and the sword. Famine begins when the average human lifespan falls to thirty years. At that time, fine food can no longer be found at all, and people boil old bones together for their meals. If one happens upon a single grain of rice, wheat, millet, or barnyard grass, it is treasured like a precious jewel, hidden away and carefully guarded.

items.zh: 彼諸有情多無氣勢，蹎僵在地不復能起。由此飢儉，有情之類亡沒殆盡。此之儉災經七年七月七日七夜，方乃得過。彼諸有情復共聚集，起下厭離。由此因緣，壽不退減，儉災遂息。
items.en: Beings, mostly without strength, collapse to the ground and cannot rise again. Through this famine, beings very nearly perish altogether. This calamity of famine lasts seven years, seven months, seven days, and seven nights before it finally passes. Beings then gather together and give rise to a rudimentary sense of renunciation; through this, their lifespan ceases to decline, and the famine comes to an end.

items.zh: 又若人壽二十歲時，本起厭患今乃退捨。爾時多有疫氣、障癘、災橫、熱惱相續而生。彼諸有情遇此諸病，多悉殞沒。如是病災經七月七日七夜，方乃得過。
items.en: Further, when the average human lifespan falls to twenty years, the renunciation that had earlier arisen is abandoned once again. At that time, epidemics, pestilence, disasters, and feverish afflictions arise one after another. Beings who encounter these illnesses mostly perish. This calamity of disease lasts seven months, seven days, and seven nights before it finally passes.

items.zh: 彼諸有情復共聚集，起中厭離。由此因緣，壽量無減，病災乃息。
items.en: Those beings then gather together once more, and a middling sense of disenchantment arises in them. Because of this, their lifespan declines no further, and the calamity of disease comes to an end.

items.title: The Third Minor Calamity — the Sword, and the Eon of Abiding Completed

items.zh: 又人壽十歲時，本起厭患今還退捨。爾時有情展轉相見，各起猛利殺害之心。由此因緣，隨執草木及以瓦石，皆成最極銳利刀劍，更相殘害，死喪略盡。如是刀災極經七日，方乃得過。
items.en: Further, when the average human lifespan falls to ten years, the renunciation that had arisen is abandoned once again. At that time, beings, encountering one another, each give rise to a fierce intent to kill; through this, whatever grass, wood, tiles, or stones they grasp all become the sharpest of blades, and they slaughter one another until nearly all have perished. This calamity of the sword lasts at most seven days before it finally passes.

items.zh: 爾時有情復有三種最極衰損。謂壽量衰損、依止衰損、資具衰損。壽量衰損者，所謂壽量極至十歲。依止衰損者，謂其身量極至一搩，或復一握。資具衰損者，爾時有情唯以粟稗為食中第一，以髮毼為衣中第一，以鐵為莊嚴中第一。五種上味悉皆隱沒，所謂酥、蜜、油、鹽等味，及甘蔗變味。
items.en: At that time, beings suffer three extremes of decline: decline in lifespan, decline in bodily support, and decline in material resources. Decline in lifespan means a lifespan that reaches, at most, ten years. Decline in bodily support means bodies that reach, at most, the span of a hand's width, or even just a fist's breadth. Decline in material resources means that beings then consider coarse grain the finest of foods, rough hair the finest clothing, and iron the finest ornament; the five superior flavours — butter, honey, oil, salt, and the taste of sugarcane — have all vanished entirely.

items.zh: 爾時有情展轉聚集，起上厭離，不復退減。又能棄捨損減壽量惡不善法，受行增長壽量善法，由此因緣，壽量、色力、富樂、自在皆漸增長，乃至壽量經八萬歲。如是二十減、二十增，合四十增減，便出住劫。
items.en: At that time, beings gather together and give rise to the highest degree of renunciation, never again to decline. They abandon the unwholesome practises that diminish lifespan, and take up the wholesome practises that increase it. Through this, lifespan, physical vigour, wealth, and ease of life all gradually increase once more, up to a lifespan of eighty thousand years. In this way, twenty periods of decrease and twenty periods of increase, forty in all, together complete the eon of abiding.

blocks.text: Today's reading is Buddhist cosmology: the great calamities that destroy the world, the length of an eon, and the rise and fall of the human lifespan through famine, disease, and war. It can feel remote from a treatise on the mind. Keep two points in view as you read. First, all of this is presented as the result of beings' karma, so it belongs to the mental consciousness's powers. Second, the moral engine of the story is renunciation: each time things recover, it is because beings themselves turn away from harm.

One sentence is missing from Ru-Yi's translation (now supplied in our own translation, marked as ours) (0285c29–0286a02): after the epidemic, beings gather again and give rise to a middling degree of renunciation, their lifespan stops declining, and the plague ends.

subs.head: The world's span is fixed; ours is not

blocks.text: The world's lifespan is fixed at one eon, but a being's lifespan "is not fixed", because beings make so many kinds of karma: it may last longer than an eon or as little as a year. Venerable Miào Jìng's example of "longer than an eon": a being suffering in hell for slandering the Dharma does not go free when this world ends; it continues its suffering in another world.

The world is destroyed by **fire**, which reaches up to the Brahmā heavens (the first dhyāna); by **water**, up to the second dhyāna; and by **wind**, up to the third. The fourth dhyāna is destroyed by none of them, because its gods arise and cease together with their palaces.

Both teachers cite the *Mahāvibhāṣā* for why each level falls to its calamity: inner faults answer to outer calamities. Below the first dhyāna there is investigation and analysis, and much thinking is like fire. The second dhyāna has joy, which is like water. The third has bliss and still has breathing, and breath is wind. The fourth has no breath, so nothing can destroy it. The cosmology mirrors the states of meditation.

Twenty **intermediate eons** (中劫) each for destruction, emptiness, formation, and abiding make eighty, which are "provisionally called one great eon" (大劫). In the Brahmā heavens "one eon" is scaled to rank: twenty intermediate eons for the multitude of Brahmā, forty for his ministers, sixty for Great Brahmā himself.

A warning for reading other texts, from Venerable Miào Jìng: older translations call one decrease-and-increase "a small eon", twenty of those "an intermediate eon", and four intermediate eons "a great eon". The *Yogācārabhūmi* calls one decrease-and-increase "an intermediate eon". The total length is the same; only the names differ. Check which naming a text uses before comparing figures.

subs.head: The rise and fall of the human lifespan

blocks.text: At first the human lifespan is "unlimited". Venerable Miào Jìng, citing the *Mahāvibhāṣā*, notes that this means extremely long, not infinite: no karma done with a scattered desire-realm mind yields more than one eon. The lifespan falls to eighty thousand years, then, "because beings take up unwholesome practices", down to ten, then rises again as beings take up wholesome ones. Master Cháng Bǎi: the cycle "runs on a moral engine"; it tracks beings' own conduct, never an outside force.
As the lifespan falls, three **minor calamities** strike, and Venerable Miào Jìng explains the difference from the great ones: great calamities destroy the world, minor ones destroy beings.

items: At thirty years, **famine**, lasting seven years, seven months, seven days, and seven nights. People boil old bones for food.
At twenty years, **disease**: epidemics and fevers, lasting seven months, seven days, and seven nights.

At ten years, **the sword**: meeting one another, beings conceive a fierce intent to kill, and whatever they pick up, grass or stone, becomes a blade. It lasts at most seven days. Master Cháng Bǎi calls it the worst of the three, because it is driven by hatred itself.

blocks.text: Each ends the same way: beings gather and give rise to **renunciation** (厭離): rudimentary after the famine, middling after the plague (the sentence missing from Ru-Yi), and the highest after the sword, "never again to decline". They give up the unwholesome practises that shorten life and take up those that lengthen it. Venerable Miào Jìng: "it still comes down to their own thought and conduct, not something heaven did." Master Cháng Bǎi: there is no external rescue, only beings growing weary enough of harm to change.

At the lowest point beings suffer three declines: of lifespan (ten years at most), of body (a hand's width or a span), and of resources. Then the long recovery begins. Twenty decreases and increases complete the eon of abiding. Venerable Miào Jìng adds that the count is a round figure: the first period only decreases and the last only increases.

quiz.q: The treatise says the duration of the physical world is fixed. What about the lifespans of beings?
options: also exactly one eon
always eighty thousand years
not fixed — because beings create many kinds of karma, a lifespan may exceed an eon, or be reduced to as little as a year
always one hundred years
quiz.why: "As for the lifespans of beings, however, their duration is not fixed. Why is this? Because beings create karma of many different kinds, a lifespan may exceed a full eon, or may be reduced to as little as a single year." Venerable Miào Jìng's example of "exceeding an eon": one who slanders the Dharma, suffering in hell, goes on suffering in another world when this one is destroyed; "as little as a year" also covers a month or a day. Master Cháng Bǎi: some die as soon as they enter the womb.

quiz.q: How far does each of the three calamities reach?
options: fire from the hell of uninterrupted suffering up to the Brahmā heavens; water up to the second dhyāna; wind up to the third dhyāna; the fourth dhyāna is destroyed by no calamity
all three reach the fourth dhyāna
fire reaches farthest, up to the formless realm
wind destroys only the desire realm
quiz.why: "The first is fire, which destroys the world from the hell of uninterrupted suffering up to the Brahmā heavens. The second is water, which destroys everything up to the second dhyāna heaven. The third is wind, which destroys everything up to the third dhyāna heaven. The fourth dhyāna heaven is destroyed by no calamity at all," because its gods arise and cease together with their palaces. Venerable Miào Jìng: the three great calamities destroy the world, not beings — the beings have already left before they come.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, how many intermediate eons make up one great eon?
options: twenty
forty
eighty — twenty each for destruction, emptiness, formation, and abiding
one hundred
quiz.why: "Twenty intermediate eons make up the eon of destruction; twenty more, once destroyed, make up the eon of emptiness; twenty more make up the eon of formation; and twenty more, once formed, make up the eon of abiding. These eighty intermediate eons together are provisionally called one great eon." Note "provisionally": the great eon is a count set up over four periods. A is one period; B is the "eon" of Brahmā's ministers.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, how does the human lifespan change within an intermediate eon, and what drives it?
options: from eighty thousand years down to ten, then back up to eighty thousand; it falls because beings take up unwholesome practices, and rises because they gain renunciation and take up wholesome ones
from one hundred up to one thousand
it never changes
the gods decide its rise and fall
quiz.why: "Then, because beings take up unwholesome practices, their lifespan decreases further, down to ten years. Then, having gained a mind of renunciation, they take up wholesome practices, and through this their lifespan gradually increases again, up to eighty thousand years." Master Cháng Bǎi: the cycle runs on a moral engine — it tracks nothing but beings' own moral condition, never an external imposition. D is precisely what this denies.

quiz.q: What are the three minor calamities that occur within an intermediate eon?
options: fire, water, and wind
earthquake, tsunami, and typhoon
famine, disease, and the sword
greed, hatred, and delusion
quiz.why: "Further, within this intermediate eon, three minor calamities occur: famine, disease, and the sword." A lists the three great calamities that destroy the world. Venerable Miào Jìng: the great calamities destroy the world; the minor ones destroy beings.

quiz.q: How does each minor calamity come to an end? The two teachers agree.
options: beings gather and give rise to renunciation — rudimentary after famine, middling after disease, the highest after the sword; not heaven's doing, but beings' own thought and conduct
the gods send relief
they stop on their own when time runs out
a king orders them to stop
quiz.why: After famine beings "give rise to a rudimentary sense of renunciation"; after the sword, "the highest degree of renunciation, never again to decline." Venerable Miào Jìng: "When everyone talks it over, it still comes down to their own thought and conduct — not something heaven did, not the old man in the sky." Master Cháng Bǎi: each ends the same way — no external rescue, but beings growing weary enough of suffering to turn towards goodness. He adds that offering a bowl of food to the Sangha keeps one from being born in an eon of famine.
